study.title: Jeremiah 9: I am sorry, judgment, and true glory
study.overview: Jeremiah 9 gathers prophetic lament, denunciation of Judah's sin, and the proclamation of God's judgment. The chapter begins with the intense pain of the prophet before the ruin of his people and continues with the description of a society marked by lies, betrayal and idolatry. Then the Lord explains that the devastation comes in response to the refusal of his law. The text culminates in the convocation to the mourning and then with the correction of all false trust: neither wisdom, nor strength, nor wealth, nor even external signs of religious belonging, replace the knowledge of the Lord, who acts with goodness, judgment, and justice. The closure extends the scope of judgment to Judah and the neighboring nations, showing that the external covenant is not enough without a heart really surrendered to God.

outline.title: The Prophet weeps ruin and denounces a lie people
outline.explanation: Jeremiah expresses a deep lament, desiring endless tears for the calamity of his people. At the same time, he describes the moral corruption of Judah: falsehood, deception, betrayal between neighbors and a practical refusal to know the Lord. Language is strong to show that disaster is not accidental, but linked to a rotten social and spiritual fabric.

outline.title: God announces proof, desolation, and exile as a righteous judgment
outline.explanation: The Lord declares that he will prove and merge his people, an image of refining by fire. The liar language, false peace and confidence in cunning itself receive sentence. The chapter then paints the desolation of the earth and explains the cause: abandonment of the law of the Lord, disobedience to his voice and follow-up of the Baalins. The result will be food of bitterness, dispersion between nations and persecution by the sword.

outline.title: Call to grief and description of general lament
outline.explanation: As judgment is inevitable, mourner women are summoned to teach crying to others. The scene is of irreparable losses: ruined houses, national shame and death even entering the palaces. The text uses images of cadavers scattered in the field to show the extent of the destruction and the total absence of those who collect the dead.

outline.title: The One True Glory and the Judgment upon All Nations
outline.explanation: God corrects all human boasting: wisdom, strength, and wealth are no reason for pride. Legitimate pride is in understanding and knowing the Lord, whose joy is to do goodness, judgment and justice. Finally, the Lord announces judgment against circumcised and uncircumcised nations, showing that the external sign is not sufficient; without obedience and faithfulness of the heart, even Israel is counted as uncircumcised in the heart.

study.context: The comments provided deal with Jeremiah 9 as part of a great judgmental discourse, in which the prophet laments the imminent ruin of Judah and Jerusalem, while the Lord presents the accusations and judgment. Tyndale notes that in the central verses, the prophet interrupts the divine discourse to respond in regret, and that the chapter also calls mourners to mourn the desolation. Matthew Henry summarizes the chapter as reprobation of sin, justification of judgment, and condemnation of trust in the power itself or in the external privilege of circumcision. Adam Clarke highlights the total devastation of the land and the call of women of mourning, and emphasized that judgment reaches not only Judah, but also other nations.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter states that God judges sin in a morally coherent way: lies, betrayal, idolatry and refusal to hear his voice bring real consequences in history. The metaphor of goldsmiths and smelter suggests that judgment also has a revealing and purifying function, but here the focus lies on the sentence against a hardened community. The text combats all religious self-confidence: neither lineage, nor external sign, nor human capacities, guarantee acceptance before God. The true foundation of glory is to know the Lord in a way that molds life according to his goodness, justice, and righteousness. The final phrase about circumcision of the heart teaches that belonging to the people of God must be internal, not merely ritual or national. Thus, the chapter unites divine holiness, human responsibility, historical judgment, and the need for a faith that is real in the heart.

scholarViews.insight: The comment suggests that the comparison of languages with arcs shows a lie used on purpose to injure the next, not just casual error.
The commentator sees in this closing the denunciation of trust in anything beyond God, including the privilege of external circumcision.
The note highlights that God's judgment also reaches other nations, and that the external sign of circumcision is not worth without a corresponding heart.

questions: In what situations do I treat the truth as a weapon, as the ones Jeremiah describes in this chapter?
Have I tried to boast in gifts, resources or position, rather than really knowing the Lord?
What external religious signs in my life need to be accompanied by inner obedience and transformed heart?
study.practice: This week, examine your speech and your motivations in the light of this chapter: refuse every form of deception, ask the Lord for a teachable heart and replace self-confidence for real dependence on it. Pray with sincerity for people and situations marked by spiritual hardship, and practice concrete trust in God's goodness, justice and righteousness through daily obedience.
study.uncertainty: Verse 2 was treated by commentators as the word of Jeremiah, although Adam Clarke mentions that some interpreters attribute it to God; this was recorded as an interpretation, not as a fact of the text. The notes provided in English were summarized without adding historical data not present in them. The biblical text provided follows the numbering indicated by the user; Clarke's observation that verse 1 belongs to the previous chapter was kept only as an implicit interpretive note, without changing the requested division.
